_comment: Compare It (Excellence tier). Two mock interfaces (panel_a, panel_b) solve the same problem differently. Stage 1: pick the more effective panel ('better_panel': 'a' or 'b'). Stage 2: pick the correct 'justification_choices' entry (exactly one 'correct': true). Stage 3: pick an 'improvement_choices' entry - each has a 'tier' (excellence/merit/not_achieved) and 'feedback'; only the excellence option should correctly link the improvement to a named principle.

questions.prompt: Two sign-up screens for Kōrero Cloud handle password creation differently. Which one applies Error Prevention more effectively?

justification_choices.text: Screen A checks password rules live as the member types, catching the problem before they ever submit - Screen B only tells them after they've already tried and failed.
Screen A uses a nicer colour scheme than Screen B.
Screen A has fewer words on the page than Screen B.
Screen B's error message appears in red text.

improvement_choices.text: On Screen B, show the same live checklist as Screen A so weak passwords are caught before the member submits, not after.
improvement_choices.feedback: Correctly links the fix straight back to Error Prevention - stopping the mistake before it happens.

improvement_choices.text: On Screen B, make the 'Continue' button a brighter colour.
improvement_choices.feedback: A reasonable tweak, but it doesn't fix the underlying problem or connect to a named usability principle.

improvement_choices.text: On Screen B, remove the password field completely.
improvement_choices.feedback: That would break the sign-up process entirely - it isn't a usability improvement.

questions.prompt: Two account settings screens let a Kōrero Cloud member cancel their subscription. Which applies User Control and Freedom more effectively?

elements.text: (cancellation hidden 3 menus deep, requires contacting support)

justification_choices.text: Screen A puts 'Cancel subscription' directly on the main settings page, giving the member a clear, immediate exit - Screen B buries it and forces a support request.
Screen A has a shorter page title than Screen B.
Screen B offers billing history, which Screen A does not show here.
Screen A loads faster than Screen B.

improvement_choices.text: On Screen B, move 'Cancel subscription' onto the main settings page as a clearly labelled, one-click option, matching Screen A.
improvement_choices.feedback: Correctly links the fix to User Control and Freedom - a visible, immediate exit rather than a buried one.

improvement_choices.text: On Screen B, add a keyboard shortcut so power users can navigate the menus faster.
improvement_choices.feedback: That's Flexibility and Efficiency of Use, a different principle - it doesn't give the member an exit, just a faster route through the same maze.

improvement_choices.text: On Screen B, change the menu font to be bolder.
improvement_choices.feedback: A minor visual tweak that doesn't address the real problem: the cancellation option is still hard to find.

questions.prompt: Two search results pages on TrailFoot Outdoors show a customer's applied filters differently. Which applies Recognition Rather Than Recall more effectively?

elements.text: Filters: Size M ✕   Colour: Green ✕   Under $200 ✕
(no summary of which filters are currently applied)

justification_choices.text: Screen A shows every active filter as a visible chip the customer can see and remove - Screen B gives no reminder, so the customer must remember what they chose earlier.
Screen A found more results than Screen B.
Screen B's page loads with a smaller number in the heading.
Screen A's filters use the colour green.

improvement_choices.text: On Screen B, add the same visible filter chips as Screen A so the customer can see and adjust their filters without recalling them from memory.
improvement_choices.feedback: Correctly links the fix to Recognition Rather Than Recall - showing filters instead of requiring the customer to remember them.

improvement_choices.text: On Screen B, change 'results' to bold text.
improvement_choices.feedback: A small visual change that doesn't solve the real memory-load problem.

improvement_choices.text: On Screen B, remove the result count entirely.
improvement_choices.feedback: That removes useful information and doesn't relate to the filter-memory problem at all.
